questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Accounting is best defined as the process of
options: transporting goods to the final consumer
recording, classifying, summarizing, and interpreting financial transactions
questions.explanation: Accounting systematically records business transactions and presents them in a form useful for decision-making.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The main purpose of financial accounting is to provide information mainly to
options: customers about the price of goods only
government about the population of a country
banks about the exchange rate of currencies
owners, managers, and other interested parties about the financial performance of a business
questions.explanation: Financial accounting produces reports for owners, managers, creditors, government, and other stakeholders to assess performance and position.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The accounting concept which assumes a business will continue operating for the foreseeable future is the
questions.explanation: The going concern concept assumes the business will continue to operate normally and not be forced to liquidate in the near future.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The accounting concept requiring revenue and expenses to be recorded when they are earned or incurred, not necessarily when cash changes hands, is the
questions.explanation: The accrual concept matches revenues to the period they are earned and expenses to the period they are incurred, regardless of cash movement.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The accounting concept that requires a business to use the same accounting methods from one period to the next is the
questions.explanation: Consistency ensures accounting methods are applied uniformly over time so that financial statements remain comparable across periods.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The accounting concept advising that revenue should not be recorded until reasonably certain, but all foreseeable losses should be provided for, is the
questions.explanation: Prudence ensures that assets and profits are not overstated, and losses/liabilities are not understated, in financial statements.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The accounting concept concerned with items significant enough to influence the decisions of users of accounts is the
questions.explanation: Materiality allows minor items to be treated in the most convenient way, while significant items must be accurately reported.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The accounting concept stating that every transaction has two effects on the accounting equation is the
questions.explanation: The dual aspect concept underlies double-entry bookkeeping: every transaction affects at least two accounts.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The accounting equation is correctly expressed as
questions.explanation: The fundamental accounting equation states that a business's assets are financed either by liabilities (what it owes) or capital (owner's investment).

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: If a business has assets of ₦500,000 and liabilities of ₦200,000, its capital is
questions.explanation: Using Assets = Liabilities + Capital: 500,000 = 200,000 + Capital, so Capital = 300,000.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: In the ledger, accounts are broadly classified into
questions.explanation: Ledger accounts are traditionally grouped into personal (people/organisations), real (assets), and nominal (income/expenses) accounts.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: An account relating to individuals, firms, or organisations that the business deals with is called a
questions.explanation: Personal accounts record transactions with specific people or entities, such as debtors and creditors.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: An account relating to tangible and intangible assets of a business is called a
questions.explanation: Real accounts track assets such as cash, buildings, machinery, and goodwill.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: An account relating to expenses, losses, incomes, and gains is called a
questions.explanation: Nominal accounts record items that affect the profit and loss of a business, such as rent expense or sales revenue.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Under the double-entry rule for personal accounts, the receiver of a benefit is
questions.explanation: The rule for personal accounts is: debit the receiver, credit the giver.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Under the double-entry rule for real accounts, what comes into the business is
questions.explanation: The rule for real accounts is: debit what comes in, credit what goes out.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Under the double-entry rule for nominal accounts, all expenses and losses are
questions.explanation: The rule for nominal accounts is: debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The book in which transactions are first recorded, before being posted to the ledger, is called a
questions.explanation: Books of prime entry, such as journals and the cash book, are where transactions are first recorded chronologically.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The book of prime entry used to record credit sales of goods to customers is the
questions.explanation: The sales journal records all credit sales made to customers before they are posted to individual customer accounts.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The book of prime entry used to record credit purchases of goods for resale is the
questions.explanation: The purchases journal records all credit purchases of goods intended for resale.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The book of prime entry used to record goods returned by customers to the business is the
questions.explanation: The sales returns journal records goods that customers send back to the business, also called returns inwards.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The book of prime entry used to record goods the business returns to its suppliers is the
questions.explanation: The purchases returns journal records goods the business sends back to suppliers, also called returns outwards.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The book of prime entry used to record transactions that do not fit into any other specialised journal, such as opening entries and correction of errors, is the
questions.explanation: The general journal (journal proper) records miscellaneous entries like opening balances, error corrections, and non-routine adjustments.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: A cash book that records both cash and bank transactions in two separate columns is called a
questions.explanation: A two-column cash book has separate columns for cash and bank transactions on both the debit and credit sides.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: A cash book with columns for cash, bank, and discount is called a
questions.explanation: The three-column cash book adds a discount column (allowed on the debit side, received on the credit side) to the cash and bank columns.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Discount given to a debtor for prompt payment, recorded on the debit side of the cash book, is called
questions.explanation: Discount allowed is given by the business to its customers for early payment, reducing the amount received.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Discount received from a creditor for prompt payment, recorded on the credit side of the cash book, is called
questions.explanation: Discount received is given to the business by its suppliers for early payment, reducing the amount paid out.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The system of maintaining a small cash fund, periodically reimbursed to restore it to a fixed amount, is called the
questions.explanation: Under the imprest system, a fixed float is given to the petty cashier and topped up periodically to match the amount spent.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The petty cash book is mainly used to record
options: large capital purchases such as machinery
small, day-to-day cash expenses such as postage and stationery
questions.explanation: The petty cash book records minor recurring expenses that are impractical to pay by cheque or record in the main cash book.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Cash paid into the bank is recorded on the
options: credit side of the bank column only
debit side of both cash and bank columns
debit side of the cash column only
debit side of the bank column and credit side of the cash column in the cash book
questions.explanation: A cash-to-bank lodgement is a contra entry: debit bank (money coming into the bank) and credit cash (money leaving the till).

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: A trial balance is best described as
options: a statement showing a firm's profit for the year
a book of prime entry for cash transactions
a list of ledger balances showing whether total debits equal total credits
a statement showing a firm's assets and liabilities only
questions.explanation: The trial balance checks the arithmetical accuracy of the ledger by confirming that total debit balances equal total credit balances.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: An error where a transaction is completely omitted from the books is called an error of
questions.explanation: An error of omission occurs when a transaction is not recorded at all, so it does not affect the trial balance's agreement.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: An error where a transaction is entered in the correct class of account but the wrong person's account is called an error of
questions.explanation: An error of commission occurs when the right type of account is used, but the wrong specific account (e.g., wrong customer) is debited or credited.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: An error where a transaction is entered against the fundamental rules of accounting, such as capital expenditure treated as revenue expenditure, is called an error of
questions.explanation: An error of principle occurs when an item is recorded in the wrong class of account altogether, breaching accounting rules.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: An error where the wrong figure is used for both the debit and credit entries of a transaction is called an error of
questions.explanation: An error of original entry occurs when an incorrect amount is entered for a transaction, but the double entry is still balanced.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: An error where the debit and credit entries of a transaction are entered on the wrong sides of the correct accounts is called an error of
questions.explanation: Complete reversal happens when the correct accounts are used but the debit and credit sides are switched.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Which of the following errors would cause a trial balance to disagree?
options: Treating a capital expense as a revenue expense
Posting only one side of a transaction to the ledger
Recording a transaction in the wrong personal account
Omitting a transaction entirely from the books
questions.explanation: A one-sided entry directly breaks the equality of total debits and credits, causing the trial balance to disagree, unlike the other listed errors.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: An account opened temporarily to record the difference when a trial balance fails to balance is called a
questions.explanation: A suspense account temporarily holds the trial balance difference until the underlying errors are found and corrected.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Expenses paid in the current period but relating to the next accounting period are called
questions.explanation: Prepayments are expenses paid in advance of the period they relate to, and are treated as an asset in the balance sheet.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Expenses incurred in the current period but not yet paid are called
questions.explanation: Accrued expenses are costs that have been incurred but not yet paid, and are treated as a liability in the balance sheet.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The reduction in the value of a fixed asset due to wear and tear, age, or obsolescence is called
questions.explanation: Depreciation systematically allocates the cost of a fixed asset as an expense over its useful life.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The method of depreciation that charges an equal amount of depreciation each year over an asset's useful life is the
questions.explanation: The straight-line method spreads depreciation evenly, calculated as (Cost - Residual Value) / Useful Life.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The method of depreciation that charges a fixed percentage on the asset's book value each year, resulting in higher charges in earlier years, is the
questions.explanation: The reducing balance method applies a constant rate to the asset's remaining book value, so depreciation charges decrease over time.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Debts owed to a business that are considered irrecoverable and are written off are called
questions.explanation: Bad debts arise when a customer is unable or unwilling to pay, and the amount is written off as an expense.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: An estimated amount set aside to cover debts that may become uncollectible in the future is called
questions.explanation: A provision for doubtful debts is a prudent estimate of debts that might not be collected, reducing the receivables to a realistic value.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The account that shows the gross profit or gross loss made from buying and selling goods during a period is the
questions.explanation: The trading account calculates gross profit (or loss) as sales minus cost of goods sold.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Gross profit is calculated as
questions.explanation: Gross profit measures the profit made purely from trading activities, before deducting operating expenses.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The cost of goods sold is calculated as
questions.explanation: Cost of goods sold reflects the value of stock actually sold, found by adding purchases to opening stock and subtracting what remains unsold.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The account that shows the net profit or net loss of a business after deducting operating expenses from gross profit is the
options: profit and loss account (statement of profit or loss)
questions.explanation: The profit and loss account deducts expenses such as rent, salaries, and depreciation from gross profit to arrive at net profit.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Net profit is calculated as
options: Gross Profit + Cost of Goods Sold
Gross Profit - Operating Expenses + Other Income
questions.explanation: Net profit reflects overall profitability after accounting for all operating expenses and additional incomes, starting from gross profit.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: A statement showing a business's assets, liabilities, and capital at a specific point in time is called a
questions.explanation: The balance sheet is a snapshot of what a business owns (assets), owes (liabilities), and the owner's stake (capital) on a given date.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Assets that are expected to be converted into cash, sold, or used up within one year are called
questions.explanation: Current assets, such as stock, debtors, and cash, are short-term resources expected to be used within the normal operating cycle.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Assets held for long-term use in the business, such as land, buildings, and machinery, are called
questions.explanation: Fixed assets are long-term resources used to generate income over multiple accounting periods, not intended for resale.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Cash or goods withdrawn by the owner of a business for personal use are called
questions.explanation: Drawings reduce the owner's capital, as they represent resources taken out of the business for personal use.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The amount invested by the owner into the business, plus retained profits less drawings, represents the
questions.explanation: Capital reflects the owner's residual claim on the business's assets after all liabilities have been deducted.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: A bank reconciliation statement is prepared mainly to
options: explain the difference between the cash book balance and the bank statement balance
determine the value of closing stock
calculate the net profit of a business
questions.explanation: Bank reconciliation identifies and explains timing differences and errors between a firm's cash book and the bank's own records.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Cheques issued by a business but not yet presented to the bank for payment are called
questions.explanation: Unpresented cheques have been written and recorded in the cash book but have not yet been cashed by the payee at the bank.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Cheques or cash paid into the bank by a business but not yet recorded (credited) on the bank statement are called
questions.explanation: Uncredited lodgements have been deposited and recorded in the cash book but the bank has not yet processed and shown them on the statement.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Charges deducted directly by the bank for services rendered, which appear on the bank statement before being entered in the cash book, are called
questions.explanation: Bank charges are fees the bank deducts automatically; the business only learns of them from the bank statement and records them afterward.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: A regular, fixed payment instruction given by a customer to their bank to pay a third party is called a
questions.explanation: A standing order is a fixed instruction to the bank to pay a set amount at regular intervals to a specified payee.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: A cheque that a bank refuses to honour, usually due to insufficient funds, is called a
questions.explanation: A dishonoured cheque is returned unpaid by the bank, requiring the amount to be reversed in the drawer's cash book.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The cash book balance is adjusted for items such as bank charges and standing orders to produce the
questions.explanation: The adjusted cash book incorporates items the bank already knows about but the business has not yet recorded, arriving at the true cash book balance.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: A sales ledger control account is mainly used to
options: calculate the depreciation of fixed assets
verify the accuracy of the total balances of individual debtors' accounts
determine the cost of goods sold
questions.explanation: The sales ledger control account summarises all transactions with debtors, and its closing balance should match the total of individual debtor balances.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: A purchases ledger control account is mainly used to
options: verify the accuracy of the total balances of individual creditors' accounts
questions.explanation: The purchases ledger control account summarises all transactions with creditors, and its closing balance should match the total of individual creditor balances.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: In a sales ledger control account, cash received from debtors is recorded on the
questions.explanation: Cash received from debtors reduces what they owe, so it is credited to the sales ledger control account, which normally has a debit balance.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: In a purchases ledger control account, credit purchases from suppliers are recorded on the
questions.explanation: Credit purchases increase what the business owes to suppliers, so they are credited to the purchases ledger control account.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Control accounts help to
options: eliminate the need for a trial balance
replace the need for books of prime entry
locate errors quickly by isolating them to a particular ledger
calculate a company's net asset value
questions.explanation: By summarising a whole ledger in one account, control accounts help pinpoint which ledger contains an error when totals disagree.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: A partnership is generally defined as an association of persons carrying on business together with a view to
questions.explanation: Partnerships exist for two or more people to combine resources and skills in a joint business venture aimed at profit.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Where partners contribute capital that remains fixed unless additional capital is introduced or withdrawn, and profit-related entries pass through a separate account, the firm is using
questions.explanation: Under fixed capital accounts, capital balances stay constant while drawings, interest, salaries, and profit shares are recorded in separate current accounts.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Where all partnership transactions, including profit shares and drawings, are recorded directly in one capital account per partner, the firm is using
questions.explanation: Fluctuating capital accounts combine everything into a single account per partner, so the balance changes (fluctuates) every period.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The account used to distribute a partnership's net profit among the partners, after adjusting for salaries and interest, is called the
questions.explanation: The appropriation account shows how the net profit is shared out among partners after salaries, interest on capital, and interest on drawings are accounted for.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: In the absence of a partnership agreement, interest on partners' capital is
options: allowed at the bank lending rate
questions.explanation: Under the Partnership Act, if there is no agreement, no interest is allowed on capital contributed by partners.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Interest charged on a partner's drawings is meant to
options: reduce a partner's total capital contribution
compensate the firm for money withdrawn before it is due
increase the total profit available for appropriation
reward a partner for working harder than others
questions.explanation: Interest on drawings discourages partners from withdrawing cash early and compensates the firm for the funds' reduced availability.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: A fixed amount paid to a partner for their extra effort or specific role in the business, before profit sharing, is called a
questions.explanation: A partner's salary rewards additional responsibilities or work input and is deducted before the remaining profit is shared.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The intangible value of a business's reputation, customer base, and trading advantages above its net tangible assets is called
questions.explanation: Goodwill represents the extra value a business commands due to its reputation, location, and customer loyalty, beyond its physical assets.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: When a new partner is admitted into a partnership, goodwill is usually revalued because
options: the new partner automatically becomes the managing partner
capital accounts must always remain fixed
the new partner should compensate the old partners for the firm's existing reputation and future profit-earning potential
the business must always be dissolved first
questions.explanation: Goodwill valuation on admission ensures new partners pay fairly for the advantages built up by the existing partners before joining.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: When a partner retires from a firm, their share of goodwill is normally
options: credited to their capital account and debited to the remaining partners in their new profit-sharing ratio
written off completely with no compensation
transferred directly to the bank account
questions.explanation: On retirement, the retiring partner is compensated for their share of goodwill, usually borne by the continuing partners.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The complete winding up of a partnership business, where assets are sold and liabilities settled, is called
questions.explanation: Dissolution is the process of closing down a partnership entirely, realising its assets, and paying off its liabilities.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: On dissolution of a partnership, the account used to record the sale of assets and settlement of liabilities is called the
questions.explanation: The realisation account records the disposal of assets and payment of liabilities, with any resulting profit or loss shared among partners.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: On dissolution, if the sale of assets realises more than their book value, the resulting profit is
options: kept entirely by the managing partner
paid to the firm's creditors only
returned to customers as a refund
shared among the partners in their profit-sharing ratio
questions.explanation: Any profit or loss on realisation during dissolution is distributed among partners according to their agreed profit-sharing ratio.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: A partner who contributes capital and shares in profits but does not take part in the day-to-day management of the firm is called a
questions.explanation: A sleeping partner invests capital and shares profits/losses but stays out of active management of the business.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The document evidencing part-ownership of a limited liability company, issued in exchange for the shareholder's capital contribution, is called a
questions.explanation: A share represents a unit of ownership in a company, entitling the holder to dividends and voting rights, depending on the class of share.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: When shares are issued at exactly their nominal (face) value, they are said to be issued
questions.explanation: Shares issued at par are sold for exactly their stated nominal value, with no extra amount added or deducted.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: When shares are issued for more than their nominal (face) value, the excess is called a
questions.explanation: A share premium arises when investors pay more than the nominal value for shares, often reflecting the company's strong prospects.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: When shares are issued for less than their nominal (face) value, they are said to be issued
questions.explanation: Shares issued at a discount are sold below their nominal value, though this is subject to strict legal restrictions.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: A long-term loan capital instrument issued by a company, carrying a fixed rate of interest and not conferring ownership rights, is called a
questions.explanation: Debentures represent borrowed (loan) capital, unlike shares, which represent ownership; debenture holders are creditors, not owners.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Unlike ordinary shareholders, debenture holders receive
options: a fixed rate of interest, payable whether or not the company makes a profit
a share of the company's net assets before any other claim
a variable dividend depending on profit levels only
voting rights at the company's annual general meeting
questions.explanation: Debenture interest is a fixed obligation of the company and must be paid regardless of whether profits are made, unlike ordinary dividends.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Bookkeeping in which only a single entry, rather than a complete double entry, is made for each transaction is called
questions.explanation: Under incomplete records, not every transaction is recorded with a corresponding debit and credit, so records are less than a full double-entry system.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Where a business keeps incomplete records, the opening and closing capital can be found by preparing a
questions.explanation: A statement of affairs, similar in form to a balance sheet, is used to estimate capital at a point in time from incomplete records.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Under incomplete records, profit for the period can be estimated using the formula
options: Closing Capital + Drawings - Additional Capital Introduced - Opening Capital
questions.explanation: Profit is derived by comparing capital at the start and end of the period, adjusting for drawings taken out and additional capital put in.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Under incomplete records, total credit sales for the period can be estimated by preparing a
questions.explanation: A total debtors account reconstructs credit sales figures using known opening/closing debtor balances, cash received, and other adjustments.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: Under incomplete records, total credit purchases for the period can be estimated by preparing a
questions.explanation: A total creditors account reconstructs credit purchases using known opening/closing creditor balances, cash paid, and other adjustments.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: An organisation set up not to make a profit but to provide services to its members, such as a sports club, is called a
questions.explanation: Not-for-profit organisations, like clubs and societies, exist to serve their members' interests rather than to generate profit for owners.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: A summary of cash actually received and paid by a club during a period, similar to a cash book summary, is called a
questions.explanation: The receipts and payments account records only actual cash movements, without adjusting for accruals or prepayments.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: A statement prepared for a club, on the accrual basis, showing whether it made a surplus or deficit for the period, is called an
questions.explanation: The income and expenditure account is the not-for-profit equivalent of a profit and loss account, prepared on an accrual basis.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: In a not-for-profit organisation, the equivalent of capital, representing accumulated surpluses over the years, is called the
questions.explanation: The accumulated fund is built up from surpluses (and reduced by deficits) over time, similar to retained earnings in a trading business.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: An account prepared by a manufacturing business to determine the total cost of goods produced during a period is called the
questions.explanation: The manufacturing account calculates the production cost of goods manufactured, which then feeds into the trading account as cost of goods sold.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: In a manufacturing account, the cost of materials and labour directly traceable to production is classified as
questions.explanation: Prime cost consists of direct materials, direct labour, and direct expenses that can be directly attributed to production.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: The total production cost of goods completed during the period, transferred to the trading account, is called the
questions.explanation: Cost of production combines prime cost and factory overheads, adjusted for work-in-progress, to give the cost of goods manufactured.

questions.subject: Financial Accounting
questions.text: If manufactured goods are transferred to the trading account at a value higher than their production cost, the difference represents a
questions.explanation: A manufacturing profit arises when goods are valued for transfer at more than they actually cost to produce, reflecting an internal 'mark-up'.
